newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 20.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- KRUPP'S HOSTILE BID FOR THYSSEN PUT ON HOLD

Krupp Hoesch, the German engineering group, has agreed to put its hostile takeover bid for Thyssen on hold in the face of political pressure. The two groups are to enter into negotiations over a joint venture in the steel-making sector. If the talks are not successful within eight days, Krupp said it would resume its DM13.6bn bid for its rival. The decision follows protests from union leaders and remarks from German chancellor Helmut Kohl expressing concern at the takeover's possible impact on jobs.
-- PENGUIN REACHES DEAL OVER CLASSIC AUTHORS' ROYALTIES

Pearson's Penguin Books subsidiary has agreed to pay royalties on books by several classic authors, including Virginia Woolf and WB Yeats, whose works has come back into copyright because of a change in European law. From January 1 1996, an EU directive extended the period for which a work remains in copyright after the author's death from 50 years to 70 years. Under the deal, believed to be the first of its kind, royalties of about 10 per cent will be paid on the wholesale price of every books sold.
-- MPS CALL FOR STOCK EXCHANGE TO BE FLOATED

The House of Commons all-party Treasury select committee will issue a call Thursday for the structure of the London stock exchange to be reformed. The committee says that, in order to reflect the interests of the market as a whole, the exchange should cease to be owned by its member companies and become a listed company in its own right. One MP said, "The stock exchange has been run for the short-term interests of marketmakers rather than the maximum benefit of the London market as a whole."
-- KEEP ON TAKING EMU MEDICINE, BANKER URGES

Wim Duisenberg, the governor of the Dutch central bank and the future head of the European Monetary Institute, has warned that Emu will only create prosperity if the Maastricht treaty's strict economic conditions are met and sustained. His remarks, made in a speech to a think-tank linked to Germany's Social Democratic party, have been interpreted as a hint that the Emi would oppose membership of the single currency for countries using creative accountancy. "Countries should not look on qualification as a sprinting competition in which they do everything to reach their goal as quickly as possible," Mr Duisenburg said.
-- MAGNOX CUTS NUCLEAR LIABILITIES BY 450 MILLION STG

Magnox Electric, the state-owned nuclear utility, claims that it may be on course to eliminate its 1.3 billion stg balance sheet deficit after cutting some 450 million stg from its nuclear liabilities. The cost savings had been generated by experience gained in decommissioning nuclear power stations, Magnox said. The reduction of Magnox's liabilities would ease the group's planned acquisition by British Nuclear Fuels, which is due to be completed by the end of March 1998.
-- IOD URGES CURBS ON PAY FOR DIRECTORS

A document published by the Institute of Directors calls for shareholders to exert more pressure on companies to prevent executives being awarded excessive renumeration packages which damage the image of the business. Packages should be justified by performance and by comparison with other industries, the report says. Although the report says that the renumeration of UK directors is in line with other EU countries and below the US, it says that some packages awarded by privatised utilities have been more generous than necessary.
-- LABOUR PROMISES IT DRIVE IN SCHOOLS

Labour will endorse the recommendations of an independent enquiry Thursday and promise an information technology revolution in schools if its wins the general election. The report, drawn up by Dennis Stevenson, chairman-elect of Pearson, claims Britain's children and economy will be irreparably damaged if information technology in schools is not made a national priority. Labour is expected to propose more IT training for teachers, an increased emphasis on IT at teacher training colleges and co-operation with telecoms companies and cable operators to link schools to the Internet.
-- MERCK CUTS PRICE OF AIDS DRUG CRIXIVAN

US drugs company Merck is to cut the price of its recently- launched Aids drug, Crixivan, by 9 per cent in the UK to bring it into line with the price in other EU countries. The move is part of a campaign by pharmaceutical companies against parallel importing, whereby drugs are bought in countries where prices are low and re-imported into countries where costs are higher. "This price adjustment reflects our continued faith in the single market for pharmaceuticals in Europe and the likely introduction of a single European currency within a few years," said Per Wold Olsen, Merck's president of human health for Europe.
-- FRANCE TELECOM SEEKS STAKE IN C&W

Michel Bon, chairman of France Telecom, has confirmed that the group is considering taking a stake in Cable & Wireless Communications, the UK telecoms and cable subsidiary of the C&W group. Speaking before France Telecom announced its last results before partial privatisation, which Bon said would seek to raise between FFr30 billion (3.27 billion stg) and FFr50 billion for the French government, he also cautioned that a deal with C&W was not close.
-- UNICHEM'S LLOYDS BID COST 14.2 MILLION STG

UK drugs distributor UniChem has reported annual results for 1996 which reveal that the group's failed bid for Lloyds Chemists had cost it 14.2 million stg. Chief executive Jeffery Harris said he had no regrets about launching the bid, which lost out to a 684.1 million stg bid from German rivals Gehe. Net exceptional costs of 13.2 million stg associated with the bid pushed pre-tax profits at UniChem down from 49.4 million stg to 40.3 million stg last year.
